genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a workshop supervisor uses two ways of teaching
the first consists in showing the movement and then having it copied
the second lets the learner work it out alone before any correction
copying gives sound results within the first week
what is learnt by copying is poorly retained
working it out alone multiplies mistakes and wastes material
the learner who has searched understands the reason for each movement
faced with a new task the copier hesitates and the searcher adjusts
the trainer blends the two approaches according to the danger of the operation
text: The man who runs the workshop teaches his apprentices in two ways, and he never tires of setting one against the other. In the first, he performs the movement himself, slows down each stage and then hands the tool over to be copied. In the second, which he trusts more, the learner is left to fumble at the material alone until he asks to be put right. Copying gives clean work inside the first week, yet it leaves a thin trace in the memory. Fumbling wastes stock and breeds mistakes, and the learner who comes through it has grasped why every movement is made. Put an unfamiliar job in front of the two and the difference shows: the copier stalls, however careful, while the one who has searched shifts his grip and carries on. So the supervisor mixes the two, keeping demonstration for the dangerous work and free exploration for the joints that can hurt nobody.

units: the reviewer notes three merits and two faults in this manual for beginners
the ideas are introduced in short linked steps
this progression keeps the reader from feeling out of their depth
difficult movements are broken down into several pictures
rival books keep to a single picture for each movement
the author avoids obscure vocabulary while staying exact
the exercises offered are judged too few
the answers placed at the end of the volume do not explain the reasoning
the book is recommended to anyone who works in an orderly way
it suits badly the reader who needs constant correction
text: Three things set this manual for beginners above comparable handbooks, and two shortcomings temper the praise. Its progression comes first: it climbs in short steps, each fresh idea resting on the one before, so that the reader never feels out of their depth. Its pictures come next, breaking every awkward movement into a run of small images where rival books make do with a single shot. Its prose comes last, refusing jargon without giving up an ounce of precision. The reservations fall on two points. The exercises closing each chapter are far too few for anyone who wants real practice, and the answers, banished to the back of the volume, say nothing about how they were reached. The book therefore suits the orderly reader, and suits far less the one who learns alone and needs a constant check on his mistakes.

units: the writer of the letter addresses his former trainer
he let a long stretch of time pass before writing
at the start he applied the instructions without grasping their sense
he went over them in the evening from memory
the workshop then handed him a complete order
he spoiled his first three pieces and thought of giving up
mending the fourth piece showed him the worth of patience
he now lays out his materials the day before and writes his mistakes down
he has been asked to train a newcomer
he finds that what he inherited above all is a way of looking at error
text: I am writing at last, after a whole season of silence, to tell you what has become of your teaching in my hands. At the start I copied out your instructions without understanding them, and went over them in my head each evening like a lesson learnt by heart. Then, in the cold months, the workshop handed me an order of my own. I ruined the first three pieces and came close to walking away. It was while mending the fourth that what you used to say about patience took on a plain meaning. Since then I lay out my tools the night before, I write my mistakes in a notebook, and I read it through before every fresh batch. Last season the woman in charge asked me to start a beginner off. I heard your own words coming out of my mouth, almost without choosing them. That was when I understood: you handed me a way of looking at error.

units: explaining an idea to somebody else improves retention
a lesson left in a notebook demands no effort of memory
putting it into words aloud forces the brain to retrieve each element
this effort of recall strengthens the memory
an unexpected question brings out a gap one knew nothing about
a gap that has been spotted can then be filled
too wide a difference in level pushes the explainer to cut his account down too far
this excessive cutting distorts what he believed he had mastered
the ideal listener is slightly less advanced but able to argue back
text: Do you hold on to an idea better once you have said it to somebody else? You do, and the reason is short. While the lesson sits in a notebook, nothing asks the memory to build it again; the moment you have to put it into words aloud, the brain goes hunting for every link, and that act of retrieval deepens the trace. And if the other person asks something you did not expect? So much the better. The question opens up a hole you would never have found on your own, and a hole once seen can be filled. Should you then explain anything to anyone at all? No. Where the difference in level is huge, the one explaining cuts his account down too far, and the trimming ends up bending what he believed he had mastered. The right partner stands a step behind you, close enough to follow, fresh enough to argue back.

units: the woman running a shared workshop describes a problem of keeping people
newcomers were dropping out after three sessions
they walked home every evening with a spoiled piece of work
a volunteer craftsman saw beginners tense up at their very first cut
the team changed the way the sessions run
a newcomer now finishes a piece begun by somebody else
he takes on the finishing only
beginners leave with a completed object and come back
the craftsman thinks this choice holds back the learning of the cut
he admits that the learners stay long enough to learn it in the end
text: The woman who runs the shared workshop made no secret of the trouble when we put the question to her. Newcomers were dropping out after three sessions, she said, because they walked home every evening holding something they had spoiled. A volunteer joiner, sitting by the bench, backed her up: he could watch hands go tight at the very first cut. So the team pulled the sessions apart and built them again. Every newcomer now ends the evening on a piece somebody else began, she explained, with nothing left but the sanding and the polishing. The beginner carries home a finished object, she added, and turns up again the week after. The joiner put a qualification on it. The scheme holds back the learning of the cut, he said, but it keeps people about long enough that they learn it in the end.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: knowledge travelled by mouth and by hand before writing
spoken narration rested on the return of the same turns of phrase
the group put right the teller's slips
handwork was learnt almost without speech
no abstract rule was taught to the beginner
the apprentice copied what he saw and was corrected physically
the true movement lodged in the muscle before it was understood
writing keeps the exact wording but loses the voice and the presence
workshop transmission dies out if the craftsman trains no successor
the two ways of passing on ended by completing each other
text: Before writing froze what people knew, everything travelled by mouth and by hand, and each road had its own laws. The spoken tale lived on repetition: the teller came back to the same turns of phrase, and the memory of the listening group pulled him up when he strayed. Handwork, by contrast, hardly used speech at all. Nobody set out an abstract rule for the beginner; the apprentice watched, copied, took a rap on the knuckles, and the true movement lodged in the muscle long before it reached the head. Once carved signs spread, the comparison turned round. The written page kept the wording untouched but lost the voice, the shading, the presence of the master. The workshop kept the movement alive and went out with the craftsman who had trained nobody to follow him. In the end the two roads answered each other.

units: the author describes four levers of lasting memorisation
going over an idea at widening intervals fixes it better
a recall that is slightly awkward strengthens the memory
putting questions to yourself works better than reading the page again
rereading creates a misleading feeling of command
shuffling exercises of different kinds slows the session down
this shuffling teaches you to name the problem before choosing a method
the brain runs the learnt sequences through again during sleep
the most useful sequences move into a steadier memory
these levers do not remove the need for repetition but make it pay better
text: Four levers hold a scrap of learning in place for good. Spacing is the first: an idea gone over at widening intervals bites deeper than the same idea gone over in one sitting, since every slightly awkward recall firms up the trace. Self-testing is the second: putting questions to yourself beats reading the page again, because rereading hands you a feeling of command that nothing has tested. Shuffling is the third: mixing exercises of different kinds drags the session out, yet it trains you to name the problem before you reach for a method. Sleep is the fourth, and while you sleep the brain runs the learnt sequences through again and moves the useful ones into steadier keeping. Not one of these levers takes the place of practice repeated; each one raises what that practice returns.

units: a beginner in bookbinding is given an order that strikes her as nonsense
her trainer forbids her to stitch before she has folded an enormous quantity of sheets
she carries out the order without believing in it
she feels she is losing a whole season
her folds come out even as the weeks pass
her fingers end by sensing the thickness of the paper without measuring
once allowed to sew she gets a straight spine and clean stitching
the trainer owns up to having been through the same ordeal and loathed it
he explains that this drudgery trains the hand and not the craft itself
a hand already schooled picks up the next movement without a struggle
text: In her first winter the young binder was given an order she took for nonsense. The master of the workshop forbade her to stitch a single section until she had folded a mountain of sheets by hand. She did as she was told and believed none of it, sure that a whole season was going to waste. Week by week her folds came out even, and then her fingers gave up measuring altogether: they felt the thickness of the paper and stopped where they should. When she was let loose on the sewing at last, the thread ran along a spine that was already straight, and not one stitch buckled. The master owned up then. He had been through the same ordeal, he said, and had loathed every hour of it. The drudgery taught nobody how to bind; it taught the hand, and a hand already schooled takes the next movement without a struggle.

units: the method starts by cutting the piece into short stretches
a memory loaded past its limit takes in nothing
a stretch of two bars lodges better than a whole page
each stretch must first be played at a slow pace
a mistake repeated beds down as firmly as a sound movement
two stretches are to be tied together once one comes out clean three times running
breakdowns happen above all at the seams between stretches
the session closes with a run of the whole thing however rough
the next day it is better to start again at the seams than at the opening
ignoring this advice leaves the opening solid and the ending shaky
text: Cut the piece into short stretches before you do anything else, because a memory loaded well past its limit takes in nothing at all: a couple of bars will lodge where a whole page simply runs away. Play each stretch slowly to begin with, since a mistake repeated beds down every bit as firmly as a sound movement, and dropping the speed keeps the fault from settling in. Once a stretch comes out clean three times running, tie it to the one beside it, for a piece gives way at the seams far more often than it does in the middle of a phrase. Close the session with a run of the whole thing, rough as it may be, so that the memory holds an outline of the shape. Next day, start again at the seams rather than at the opening, or the first bars will gleam and the ending will stay shaky right up to the concert itself.

units: a converted shed houses a neighbourhood workshop
people living nearby saw that the craftsmen who retired carried their trade off with them
the young people round about had nowhere to train
an association put together a scheme with nothing clever about it
each retired volunteer gives two half sessions a week
he takes on two beginners at most
there is neither a syllabus nor an examination
the starting point is a repair brought in by a neighbour
half of the beginners come back from one season to the next
the old hands say that explaining makes them take apart movements that had gone automatic
text: There is sanding, sawing and loud argument going on in the converted shed at the bottom of the road. Everyone living nearby knew the problem: the craftsmen who retired were carrying their trade off with them, and the young people round about had nowhere to pick anything up. An association put together a scheme with nothing clever about it. Each retired volunteer comes in two afternoons a week and takes on two beginners, no more than that. No syllabus, no examination: you start from whatever a neighbour has brought in, a wobbly chair, a shutter that sticks, and the old hand shows you as you go. The results caught the association itself off guard. Half the beginners come back from one season to the next. The old hands gain as well, since explaining makes them take apart movements that had gone automatic.
